info.name: Bank API
info.description:
Customers, accounts and sign-in against the Spring Boot API. Nine folders, run in order.

REPEATABLE BY CONSTRUCTION: every folder deletes whatever it creates and never changes a seeded record to a different value, so the collection can be run twice in a row and leaves the database exactly as it found it. Baseline it expects: customer 3 (carol), customer 4 (admin, the only ADMIN), and accounts 101, 102, 103. All money is moved on accounts the collection creates and then deletes, so no seeded balance is ever touched.

ASSERTS BODIES, NOT ONLY STATUS. Several of the guarantees here - a balance that cannot be set by a client, a role that cannot be smuggled in, a password that survives an edit - return an ordinary 200 or 201 whether they hold or not. A status-only suite cannot see any of them, which is exactly how the defects in folders 6 and 9 reached production.

Was 'Bank API - Phase 2' and covered customers only. Renamed because the customer-only scope was the thing being corrected.

item.name: 1 - happy path
item.description: Full customer lifecycle. Creates a customer, edits it and deletes it again, so the folder leaves the database exactly as it found it. The server assigns the id, so it is captured from the create response rather than hardcoded - an earlier version of this collection sent its own id, which the API no longer accepts.

pm.test('the seeded customer is the one returned', () => pm.expect(c.username).to.eql('carol'));
pm.test('accountIds is a list, never null', () => pm.expect(c.accountIds).to.be.an('array'));

pm.test('the edited name came back', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().fullName).to.eql('Nina C. Ortez'));

item.name: 2 - not found (404)
item.description: Absence is a 404 on every verb. Id 99 is not seeded and nothing in this collection creates it.

exec: pm.test('404, not 201 - PUT does not create', () => pm.response.to.have.status(404));

item.name: 3 - conflict (409)
item.description: State-dependent refusals. Each would succeed against a different database, which is what separates a 409 from a 400. Both rules here hold for EVERY caller including curl, because they ask about the state of the system rather than about who is asking.

request.description: The caller cannot pick an id, so the username is the only thing two creates can collide on. This request replaced a 'duplicate id' one, which is no longer expressible - CreateCustomerRequest has no id field.

exec: pm.test('409, not 400 - the failure is state-dependent', () => pm.response.to.have.status(409));

item.name: GET customers is unchanged by the refused create

request.description: The one protection in this application that is not cosmetic. 'At least one admin must remain' is an invariant about system state, so it needs no authentication and holds for curl exactly as it holds for the UI.

exec: pm.test('409 - at least one admin must remain', () => pm.response.to.have.status(409));
pm.test('200 OK - the refusal deleted nothing', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: 4 - validation (400) and what cannot be smuggled
item.description: Malformed requests, plus the structural guarantees: fields a client does not own cannot be set by sending them, because the request records have no component to bind them to. Those return 200/201 and IGNORE the extra fields - asserting the status alone would prove nothing, so each checks the stored values instead.

exec: pm.test('400 - @NotBlank rejects whitespace, @NotNull would not', () => pm.response.to.have.status(400));
pm.test('405 - routing table keys on verb + path', () => pm.response.to.have.status(405));

item.name: POST with id and role smuggled into the body

request.description: No caller can set a role anywhere in this API. Not a check that strips it - CreateCustomerRequest has no role component, so there is nowhere for one to arrive.

exec: pm.test('201 - the extra fields bind to nothing and are ignored', () => pm.response.to.have.status(201));
pm.test('the smuggled role did NOT take effect', () => pm.expect(c.role).to.eql('CUSTOMER'));
pm.test('the smuggled id did NOT take effect', () => pm.expect(c.id).to.not.eql(99));
pm.test('204 - folder cleans up after itself', () => pm.response.to.have.status(204));

item.name: PUT with id, role and password smuggled

request.description: Sends carol's OWN username and fullName, so the request is a no-op on the fields it is allowed to change and the folder leaves her exactly as found. Everything else in the body is ignored.

exec: pm.test('200 - the extra fields bind to nothing', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('id still the path id', () => pm.expect(c.id).to.eql(3));
pm.test('role NOT promoted to ADMIN', () => pm.expect(c.role).to.eql('CUSTOMER'));
pm.test('accountIds NOT overwritten by the echoed list', () => pm.expect(c.accountIds).to.eql([103]));

item.name: POST sign in as carol, password not overwritten

request.description: The proof that the smuggled password above changed nothing. Without this the previous request could pass while having quietly destroyed the credential.

exec: pm.test('200 - the smuggled password did not take effect', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: 8 - sign in
item.description: POST /customers/signin compares a username and password and returns that customer. It is NOT authentication: no session is created and no token is issued, so the next request is as anonymous as this one and every other endpoint is reachable without signing in at all.

item.name: POST sign in as a customer

request.description: Credentials come from collection variables so the collection can be pointed at another database without editing requests. They are not secret - these are the seed credentials and they are already in committed source, in plaintext, which is a known and deliberate Phase 10 deferral rather than an oversight.

9 - regression: username uniqueness on rename
item.description: A rename could put a second customer onto an existing username. findByUsername returns a single Optional, so two matches make it throw and sign-in answers 500 - for the ORIGINAL user as much as the impostor. Any anonymous caller could lock a real user out permanently without touching that user's record. Uniqueness was enforced on create and nowhere else.
